stem: An older adult on the first postoperative day is newly withdrawn, unusually drowsy, and has difficulty sustaining attention. A staff member says, ‘The client is probably just tired because they are not agitated.’ Which action should the nurse take?

options.A: Use a validated delirium screening approach and assess for reversible contributors because delirium can present with hypoactive, quiet symptoms
options.B: Document normal postoperative fatigue because delirium requires agitation or combativeness
options.C: Wait until hallucinations develop before assessing for delirium
options.D: Assume the change is permanent cognitive decline because delirium does not usually have an acute onset

rationale: Postoperative delirium is an acute change in mental status and may be hyperactive, hypoactive, or mixed. Hypoactive delirium can appear as withdrawal, lethargy, inattention, or altered level of consciousness and is easily missed. Older surgical adults should be screened with a validated approach and evaluated for contributing causes rather than waiting for agitation.
educational_objective: Recognize hypoactive postoperative delirium and initiate appropriate screening and evaluation rather than relying on agitation as the defining sign.
source_document_title: ACS Geriatric Surgery Verification Hospitals Screen Nearly All Older Surgical Patients for Delirium, Study Finds
source_locator: Delirium is an acute mental-status change; validated screening examines inattention, disorganized thinking and altered level of consciousness; hypoactive delirium may present as withdrawal or lethargy
source_claim_supported: Older postoperative clients may have hypoactive delirium without agitation and should be screened using validated tools.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity — acute confusion/delirium, cognitive changes and therapeutic management
correction_summary: Replaced a generic risk-factor recall item with a 2026-current recognition/screening scenario focused on commonly missed hypoactive delirium. Removed the oversimplified claim that anesthesia exposure itself explains delirium.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: ACS 2026 older-adult surgical delirium evidence verified.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: Acute onset, hypoactive presentation and validated screening are directly supported.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; delirium need not be agitated.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; delirium is acute and potentially reversible.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A recognizes the clinical pattern and appropriate next action.
audit_findings.cueing: All choices interpret the same mental-status change.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Checked residual anesthesia, sleep deprivation, depression, dementia and hypoactive-delirium overlap; acute change plus inattention supports screening rather than diagnostic certainty.
